_comment: Independent-implementability ledger (SPEC §13). One record per blind
implementation attempt. This file is an ASSERTION about runs that happened;
scripts/check-implementability.py machine-checks the half that can be checked
— that each surface_digest is exactly what blind-export.py reproduces from the
recorded source — and enforces the structural rules §13 states. The verdict
itself is attested by the implementer and cannot be re-derived by CI, which is
why it carries the evidence pointer rather than standing alone.
Rounds are append-only. A superseded verdict is never edited: it is a fact
about a surface that existed, and later repair does not make it untrue.

rounds.research_question: Does the implementability methodology GENERALISE across independently evolved sections? Four rounds matured §12 and each found a new defect class, but the methodology was validated only on the section receiving all the attention. §8.6 is the harder test: 8/18 obligations witnessed, one prior blind implementation, much older design decisions, and dense interaction with identity, signatures, journals and conformance. If the method depends on licensing it should visibly fail here.
rounds.hypothesis: §8.6, on this surface, is NOT yet independently implementable without inference — predicted from its lower witnessed coverage, not from any audit. The stronger claim under test is not about §8.6 at all: it is that the METHOD produces the same quality of finding on a section it was not developed against.

taxonomy_hypothesis.claim: Every finding will fall into one of the four defect classes §12 produced. A FIFTH class would be the more valuable outcome: it would show the taxonomy is §12-shaped rather than general.
classes: 1. MISSING MEANING — the document does not say enough to proceed honestly
2. HIDDEN NORMATIVE INPUTS — meaning exists but lives in fixtures or implementation, not the declared surface
3. INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY — enough is communicated to implement, but the document contradicts itself or leans on undocumented constants
4. INCOMPLETELY DEFINED OBJECTS — every field is correct and the encoding still does not say what it identifies
taxonomy_hypothesis.method: The taxonomy is deliberately WITHHELD from the dispatch brief. Supplying it would shape what the subject looks for and convert a test of the taxonomy into a confirmation of it. Findings are classified afterwards, by us, against the list recorded here.

rounds.prediction: Specific pre-registered guess, recorded so it can lose: §8.6.4a requires rejecting a small-order public key and neither lists the encodings nor states how to derive them, so a blind implementation cannot obtain them from the surface. That would be class 2 (hidden normative inputs) — the same class round two found in §12, appearing independently in a section developed years apart. Noted BEFORE dispatch and deliberately NOT repaired first, since pre-repairing is teaching to the test.

interpretation.why: Deciding how to READ each possible outcome after seeing one is the same defect as writing a hypothesis after the result. Recorded here so no outcome can be reframed into a success, and so a clean result cannot be quietly discounted as a null one.
interpretation.what_generalisation_requires: NOT that the same defects recur. That is the weaker claim, and the recurrence prediction below tests only it. Generalisation requires the PROCESS to expose specification insufficiency on a section it was not developed against, without relying on licensing-specific machinery and without prior hints.

readings.class 2 reproduces (small-order or other: a defect class found in §12 recurring in an independently evolved domain — evidence the taxonomy is general rather than §12-shaped
readings.all findings map onto the four classes: the taxonomy holds on a section it was not derived from; stronger than any individual recurrence
readings.a FIFTH class appears: the most valuable outcome. The taxonomy was §12-shaped and is now larger. Record the new class and re-examine §12 for instances of it
readings.genuinely inference-free PASS: POSITIVE, not null. It would show the method can DISTINGUISH a mature section from an immature one rather than mechanically generating findings — which is the failure mode a process like this is most at risk of. Only counts if the derivation log holds up: expert knowledge filling a silent spec is inference, and a correct implementation built from undocumented prior knowledge is still evidence the specification was insufficient
readings.the methodology itself breaks on §8.6: a real result, not a failed run. It would mean the method depends on properties §12 happened to have — most likely a fixture family that cannot express what the section does, which §12 already hit once at LICENSE-CLOSURE-EXCLUSIVE

rounds.research_question: Does an unseen reader derive the SAME authority model from §8.7 alone, in the places where a reasonable instinct pulls the other way? The section was written immediately after the implementation, by the implementation's author, and has never been independently read.
rounds.hypothesis: §8.7 is sufficient to derive the authority model without inference. Predicted PASS on the encoding and the acceptance rules; the risk is concentrated in the four distinctions where the intuitive reading is wrong.
rounds.prediction: Seven pre-registered failure points, recorded BEFORE dispatch so a hit cannot be claimed retrospectively: (1) substring vs first-segment prefix matching; (2) capture PREVENTION vs RETENTION when a prior exact-name owner sits beneath a newly reserved prefix; (3) first publication vs first reservation as the source of prefix authority; (4) authority revision vs name revision; (5) signed authority vs external identity/endorsement; (6) unreservable prefix vs forbidden publication; (7) whether 'protocol root' is read as unreservable, protected, or both — the correct derivation is deliberately unintuitive: it prevents reservation, does NOT itself protect exact-name publications, and leaves those to ordinary exact-name policy. (7) is the one I expect to be filled in from intuition, because writing the test for it corrected my own expectation.
rounds.note: First round dispatched as a PROTOCOL KIT rather than a repository export. No reference implementation is supplied at all — not oath/, not oathrs/, no tests, no conformance script. Round 6 found that a conformance harness inside the supplied surface restated the rule under test; a source checkout cannot avoid that for a task this small, so the kit is assembled from a normative surface instead of filtered down from a tree. The subject is given a neutral journal model and a signature-verification interface, so surrounding code cannot leak behaviour. DERIVATION.md must be written BEFORE the vectors are opened, preserving the distinction between deriving the rule and tuning to examples.
rounds.prediction_outcome: LARGELY WRONG, informatively. Six of seven pre-registered points were DERIVED correctly from the text; (2) retention-vs-denial was singled out by the subject as the best-specified rule in the section, because its normative reasoning made it "impossible to implement backwards" — the decision to put the argument IN the normative text is vindicated. (7), the point I most expected to be filled in from intuition, was not a defect. The real failures were in the AUTHORITY STATE MACHINE, about which I pre-registered nothing: what `authority` contains, what revision an accepted reservation produces, and how a tie the spec itself says is reachable resolves. I predicted failures of INTERPRETATION and got failures of DEFINITION.
inferred: what `authority` CONTAINS — a pubkey or a hash of the prior reservation. Both are 64 hex; the sentinel wording implies a key, the stated `parent` analogy implies a hash, and the section never picks
the successor relation for `authority_rev` — whether an accepted reservation yields rev+1 or leaves it unchanged. Both satisfy every published sentence
how a tie at revision 0 resolves, in the concurrent state §8.7.6 itself admits is reachable
which journal `kind` and `status` values count as an accepted reservation — neither §8.2.1 nor §8.7 enumerates one
how exact-name ownership is established, which RES-NO-CAPTURE and RES-MOST-SPECIFIC both depend on: envelope author, entry pubkey, or author_pubkey, and whether it moves on re-publication
whether hex is case-sensitive; §8.7.2 omits the lowercase rule §8.6.1 states
whether §8.6.1's value-character rule and trailing-LF rule apply to this envelope
check ORDER — no vector pins it, and first-come-before-signature leaks prefix occupancy to unauthenticated submitters while passing every vector
contamination: HARNESS DEFECT, disclosed by the subject: the dispatched session carried this project's CLAUDE.md and memory index in its system prompt, which the subject did not choose to load. The kit was clean; the SESSION was not. Concretely, the string "blocked" in the subject's status vocabulary came from that context rather than from the excerpt, which publishes no status value at all. The subject notes this does not change defect D4 — it IS D4, and being able to populate a plausible vocabulary from memory is exactly what would make a round look more successful than the text warrants

no prior knowledge of §8.7 itself: namespace reservation, prefix authority, protocol roots, oath-reserve/1 and the RES-* rules appear nowhere in the leaked context, and the subject had never seen the implementation
findings: D1 (severe): `authority`'s value space is never defined — the one member the compare-and-swap compares has no stated domain, and under the hash reading no hash function or pre-image is given
D2 (severe): the successor relation for `authority_rev` is never stated. The pair is defined as what a reservation REPLACES; nothing says what it PRODUCES
D3 (severe): §8.7.4's resolution is not total over a state §8.7.6 says is reachable — two first reservations tie at revision 0 with no tie-break, and one journal yields two different holders
D4 (severe): RES-DERIVED mandates replay over a vocabulary that is not published — no `kind` or `status` value is enumerated anywhere in the supplied surface. A blacklist reading FAILS OPEN
D5 (severe): exact-name ownership is load-bearing for RES-NO-CAPTURE and RES-MOST-SPECIFIC and is defined nowhere; §8.6.5 explicitly warns the candidate keys can differ

D6: the compare-and-swap pair is motivated by transfer, which §8.7.6 says does not exist in this version — so `authority` can only ever be non-`-` for a same-key re-reservation the text never says is permitted
D7: the ABA claim asserts a property about a prefix 'returning to a key that held it before', which no operation in this version can produce
D8: §8.7.2 copies §8.6.1's design but not its value constraints — no character rule, no lowercase rule, no statement that the trailing LF is inside the signed octets
D9 (§8.2.1): the `seq` parenthetical is dead text under one reading and operative under another, giving different chain hashes for entry 0

VECTOR COVERAGE (self-inflicted): 10 of 14 normative rules are unwitnessed. Every defect above lives in the unwitnessed region. The vectors carry no journal, no prior state and no acceptance verdict, so RES-SIGNED, RES-AUTHORITY-CURRENT, RES-FIRST-COME, RES-NO-CAPTURE, RES-DERIVED, RES-MOST-SPECIFIC, RES-NEVER-INFERRED, RES-PROSPECTIVE and RES-ROOT-CONSTRAINS-RESERVATION-ONLY have no witness at all — while the commit adding them claimed they were chosen to witness the derivations most likely to be got wrong

the reject vectors do not pin check ORDER — each fails exactly one rule, so an implementation checking first-come before signature passes all 15 while leaking occupancy
rounds.implementer_statement: Yes-with-inference, and the inference is concentrated in exactly the parts no vector witnesses. The encoding half is implementable from the text alone — 15/15 on first run with no change after opening the vectors. The authority half is not: two conformant implementations can hand the same journal to two different keys, and the corpus cannot see it.
rounds.verdict_bound: NOT A MEASUREMENT (§13 IMPL-CONTAMINATION-IS-NOT-A-MEASUREMENT, added after round 9). This run disclosed session contamination, so no PASS was ever admissible from it — that prohibition is sound and asymmetric. Its INFERENCE COUNT, however, is not a bound in either direction and must not be reported as a score or compared against another round. An earlier draft of the rule claimed the count was a LOWER bound, reasoning that contamination can only resolve ambiguities silently and never invent them. That was WRONG, and round 9 is its own counterexample: its largest finding — that §14 defers its central type to a store outside the surface — came from a subject that said it SUSPECTED such a store existed, which a clean subject would not have. Contamination inflates as well as deflates. What survives is the EVIDENCE, exactly insofar as each finding is independently verifiable from the surface itself.

supplied: fixtures/vectors.jsonl (23 vectors: 3 canonical, 7 reject, 5 covers, 8 state)
rounds.research_question: A VALIDATION round, not an open-ended search. Round 7 established that §8.7 used objects it never defined. Round 8 asks whether the new §8.7.0 definitions actually CARRY the rest of the section: can an independent reader derive the authority model and implement §8.7 without borrowing meaning from the reference kernel or from session context?
rounds.hypothesis: §8.7.0 is sufficient. Predicted PASS — the ontology now defines authority, authority revision, order, ACCEPTED, and exact-name ownership before any rule uses them, and eight state vectors witness the replay rules that had no witness in round 7.
rounds.prediction: Six narrow failure modes, recorded before dispatch: (1) are authority and exact-name owner unambiguously PRINCIPALS rather than hashes or labels; (2) does authority_rev advance on every accepted authority transition and ONLY those; (3) is 'first' derived from the serialization of accepted transitions rather than physical journal position; (4) does replay accept only cryptographically verified reservation events; (5) can registry-authored kind, author_pubkey or status labels affect authority without being covered by signed bytes; (6) do retention and most-specific-wins remain derivable now that the ontology has been introduced around them. I expect (3) to be the weakest — the distinction between committed order and byte order is stated but has no vector that could distinguish them, since a single-writer journal makes them coincide.
rounds.note: KNOWN VIOLATION OF IMPL-ISOLATED-SESSION, disclosed before dispatch rather than after. The harness cannot currently strip this project's CLAUDE.md and memory index from a dispatched session's system prompt, so the rule §13 gained today CANNOT BE SATISFIED by this harness. Round 8 therefore runs under the same contamination round 7 disclosed, mitigated only by explicit quarantine instructions and mandatory disclosure. Recording this in advance is the point: a rule whose first application is a violation is a rule about the harness, and the measurement must not be reported as though the environment were clean. Second kit round; DERIVATION.md is still required before the vectors are opened.
rounds.hypothesis_outcome: PARTLY CONFIRMED. §8.7.0 carried the section: all five ontology questions were DERIVED, both fail-open traps were closed IN THE TEXT and independently witnessed, and the subject changed nothing after opening the vectors. But three live defects remain, so the ontology repair was necessary and not sufficient.
rounds.prediction_outcome: (3) CONFIRMED, and sharper than predicted. I flagged ORDER as the weakest point because no vector could distinguish committed order from byte order. The real defect is worse: §8.2.1 carries NO commit-order member and the fixture journals have no seq at all, so the specification defined its operative term as the one thing a verifier cannot read. That is not unobservable-but-pinned; it is unimplementable, and my own IMPL-UNOBSERVABLE-PINNED rule would have mis-classified it as legitimate. (1),(4),(5),(6) derived correctly — vector 21 confirmed that a mislabelled kind changes nothing, and the subject records refusing to filter on kind from memory, which would have failed that vector. (2) failed in a way I did not predict: RES-REV-SUCCESSOR is contradicted by my own tie fixture.

rounds.research_question: Can an independent implementer derive SPEC §14's Request model from the normative PROSE ALONE and build a conforming HTTP adapter? §14 was written because the handler protocol had no normative text at all: the only statement of the rule lived in a comment in examples/http.oath, and the reference backend violated it. The section therefore has three separable claims, and this round establishes only the third — the Go adapter conforms (evidenced by an end-to-end gate), the gate distinguishes each obligation (evidenced by ten mutations, each failing distinguishably), and THE TEXT COMMUNICATES THE MODEL (evidenced by nothing yet).
rounds.hypothesis: §14 is sufficient. Predicted PASS-WITH-INFERENCE rather than PASS. The section was written in one pass by the same author who wrote the adapter, and four of its seven obligations were added only after review found the prose claiming behaviour the code did not have or could not have. Text produced that way tends to be precise exactly where a defect was found and loose everywhere else, so I expect the surface to determine the rules it was corrected into and to leave at least one boundary the implementer must decide.
rounds.prediction: Seven INTERPRETATION questions, recorded before dispatch. These are deliberately not implementation-defect predictions: the round measures whether the prose DETERMINES a reading, so each is a place two honest readers could diverge and still both claim conformance. (1) Is host a header ENTRY or a separate Request field? (2) Does the raw path include the query string, and does it preserve percent-encoding? (3) Does cross-key sorting happen BEFORE or AFTER removal of framing and Connection-nominated fields — and does the answer change the result? (4) Are Connection option delimiters HTTP OWS (SP and HTAB) only, or whatever the implementer's language calls whitespace? (5) Are header values outside the representable byte domain REJECTED or lossily decoded? (6) Are framing fields a fixed normative SET, or inherited from whatever the host library chose to keep? (7) Do repeated values under one name remain separate and ordered, or may they be joined? I expect (3) to be the weakest, because the ordering was made normative only after review found the two rules interacting, and a reader who does not construct the interacting case may never notice the question exists.
rounds.claim_scope: The export is PROSE-ONLY and carries no vectors, so a successful implementation demonstrates that THE TEXT COMMUNICATES THE MODEL. It does NOT demonstrate fixture coverage, and no §14 conformance vectors exist to be reproduced. §14.3's worked example is inside the prose and ships with it, which means a subject can check itself against one request — that is a property of the specification, not a supplied witness. Any verdict from this round must be phrased in those terms per IMPL-VERDICT-SCOPED. FURTHER NARROWED by IMPL-CONTAMINATION-IS-NOT-A-MEASUREMENT: this run disclosed contamination, so no PASS was ever admissible from it, and the count of ten is NOT a bound in either direction. Rely on the individual findings only where each is independently verifiable from the surface — I1, (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (g) and (h) all are, by reading §14; the arithmetic over them is not.

rounds.hypothesis_outcome: SPLIT — and the pre-registration was itself defective, which is recorded rather than tidied away. The hypothesis conflated two claims that its own wording contradicts: "§14 is sufficient" AND "predicted PASS-WITH-INFERENCE rather than PASS". Under §13.2 those cannot both hold — PASS-WITH-INFERENCE means precisely that the surface was NOT sufficient. Recorded honestly: (1) the SUFFICIENCY hypothesis is DISPROVED, by ten inferences, of which I1 shows the section cannot determine the value its own success criterion is stated over; (2) the VERDICT prediction was CORRECT, including its reasoning — text written in one pass by the adapter's own author is precise where a defect was found and loose elsewhere, and all four obligations added after review came back DERIVED. A pre-registration that asserts a hypothesis and simultaneously predicts its falsification cannot be scored as a single outcome; future rounds should state sufficiency and predicted verdict as separate fields.
rounds.prediction_outcome: LARGELY WRONG, and wrong in the informative direction. Six of the seven pre-registered interpretation questions were DERIVED, not inferred: host as a header entry (D13/D14), raw path including the query and preserving percent-encoding (D16), the exclusion/ASCII ordering (D9), non-representable octets refused rather than decoded (D8), framing fields as a fixed normative set (D10), and repeats separate and ordered (D4/D5). Only Connection tokenization (I5) was inferred. The specifically-named weakest point — the sorting-versus-exclusion ordering — was derived from the sentence making it normative, and the subject reported it as the mutation that killed the most tests. Predicting WHERE a text is loose is evidently much harder than predicting THAT it is, and the pre-registration is what makes that visible instead of absorbable.
inferred: I1 — the declaration of `Request` and of the header-pair constructor. §14.2 defers to "the type bound to the name Request in the store"; the store is not in the surface, and no other section declares it. THE CENTRAL ONE: §14.0 makes "two backends produce the SAME Request value" the entire obligation, and the surface does not determine what that value IS.
I2 — whether received-at is Int or Rat. "seconds since the Unix epoch" with no type; Rat is available and exact, and no rounding rule is given.

I3 — the octet→codepoint mapping for `method` and `path`. Both are Str; REQ-HEADER-OCTETS-ARE-ASCII is scoped to headers only, so a non-ASCII octet in a request target has no stated meaning and no refusal.
I4 — the replacement for obsolete line folding. The text forbids delivering it as an embedded newline and names no substitute.
I5 — how to tokenize the `connection` value. "a comma-separated list of field names" with no grammar.
I6 — several `connection` field lines. The text says "the connection field", singular, while §14 itself forbids joining repeats.
I7 — where an :authority-derived `host` entry sits in arrival order when a `host` field line is also present, which REQ-HEADER-REPEATS-PRESERVED makes significant.
I8 — whether trailer-section fields become header entries. Only the field NAME `trailer` is excluded.
I9 — the response to a message that cannot be de-framed at all.
I10 — an HTTP/1.1 absolute-form target, where the authority arrives by a third route the section does not name.
findings: (a) `Connection: close` becomes a nomination. §14 calls the value "a comma-separated list of field names"; RFC 9110 §7.6.1 defines it as connection OPTIONS, of which `close` is the canonical example and is not a field name. Read literally — which is what DERIVED means — a backend must exclude a field named `close` on essentially every HTTP/1.1 request. The text gives no way to distinguish an option from a nominated name.

(b) §14.3's worked vector is not a legal HTTP/1.1 request — it carries no Host, while REQ-HOST-IS-A-HEADER calls Host mandatory in HTTP/1.1 — and it covers half the section. Counted exactly against §14's TWELVE REQ-* obligations: four are witnessed by claim (NAMES-LOWERCASE, ORDER-LEXICOGRAPHIC, REPEATS-PRESERVED, VALUES-NOT-JOINED); two incidentally (METHOD-VERBATIM, and PATH-IS-RAW only partly, since the target carries no percent-encoding so "NOT percent-decoded" is untested); and SIX not at all — VALUE-OCTETS, OCTETS-ARE-ASCII, FRAMING-FIELDS-EXCLUDED together with its nomination sub-rule and its normative precedence over the ASCII check, HOST-IS-A-HEADER, BODY-IS-OCTETS, TIME-IS-DATA. Those six are the ones carrying the security argument. Note this is precedence between exclusion and the ASCII check, NOT REQ-HEADER-ORDER-LEXICOGRAPHIC, which the vector does witness by producing an order different from arrival order.

(c) The Str/octet rationale is narrower than the rule it justifies: it argues from "the printable US-ASCII range" and then admits HTAB (0x09), which is outside it. The rule is sound; the stated reason does not cover the exemption granted in the same paragraph.
(d) "it cannot reinstate a name excluded above" is vacuous — nomination is a removal mechanism and has no reading under which it could add an entry.

(e) The parser/adapter boundary is never drawn, and REQ-HEADER-VALUE-OCTETS depends on it: a value "crosses unchanged" while OWS removal "is parsing, not normalization", and §14 defines the adapter's input as "whatever reached it". Two backends whose host libraries strip OWS differently can both claim conformance.

(f) MUTATION FINDING, in the specification's favour. Replacing ASCII lowering with a UNICODE-aware one is an EQUIVALENT mutant under §14 — every octet on which they disagree is outside 0x20–0x7E and refuses first. But a LOCALE-aware lowering is not equivalent: a Turkish-locale mapping sends ASCII `I` to U+0131, which no refusal catches. The clause "locale- or Unicode-aware" is doing real work in exactly one of its two halves, and the subject's first test set missed it.

(g) REQ-HEADER-OCTETS-ARE-ASCII's argument — a transcoded value makes the handler verify a signature over bytes that never arrived — applies verbatim to `path`, which REQ-PATH-IS-RAW justifies with "signed schemes rely on the raw form". The section identifies the hazard, states the reasoning, applies it to one of three Str fields, and is silent on the other two.

(h) §14.3 miscounts its own coverage: the prose says "Three obligations are jointly witnessed here" and then names FOUR rule identifiers, one clause covering REQ-HEADER-REPEATS-PRESERVED and REQ-HEADER-VALUES-NOT-JOINED together. Counted exactly, §14 states twelve REQ-* obligations; the vector witnesses four by claim, two incidentally (method, and path without any percent-encoding), and SIX not at all — including every rule carrying the security argument.
